c.tagline: Home of the blues, the birthplace of rock 'n' roll, and the soul of Southern barbecue.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares start around $2.50 plus per-mile charges; app-based Uber and Lyft are widely used and usually cheaper than hailing a cab.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 311 is Memphis's non-emergency city line.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

solo.f: fine in tourist areas; night caution

avoid.reason: Elevated violent crime; caution beyond downtown/Beale St; several neighborhoods high-crime

hood_desc: The walkable core along the Mississippi riverfront, home to the neon-lit Beale Street blues clubs, the National Civil Rights Museum at the Lorraine Motel, and the Peabody ducks; the best base for first-timers who want music, history, and nightlife on foot.

A revitalized district of art galleries, indie boutiques, and buzzy restaurants south of Beale, anchored by the historic Central Station and the Arcade Restaurant; suits younger travelers wanting a creative, trolley-connected scene.

Memphis's leafy entertainment and arts heart, with the Overton Square theater and dining district, Overton Park, the Memphis Brooks Museum, and the zoo; a lively yet local base with bars, patios, and cafes.

The residential south-side district built around Graceland, Elvis Presley's mansion and estate; convenient to the airport and the ultimate base for Elvis pilgrims, though quieter and more spread out than the core.

The Poplar Avenue corridor east of Midtown: office parks, the Memphis Botanic Garden and the Dixon Gallery and Gardens, and shopping at Oak Court Mall and Laurelwood. It is the city's main hotel cluster outside downtown and suits travellers with a car.

transit.hours: MATA buses run roughly 4:30am to midnight depending on route; the vintage Main Street Trolley runs from mid-morning to around 10-11pm, later on weekends.
transit.note: Memphis is largely car-dependent; the restored vintage Main Street Trolley is handy for getting around Downtown and the riverfront, but reaching Midtown, Graceland, or East Memphis usually needs a car or ride-hail.
transit.pay: Pay cash on board (exact fare) or use a reloadable MATA fare card or the MATA transit app. A single bus or trolley ride is $1.75, a vintage Main Street Trolley ride is $1, and a day pass is about $3.50.

tip.r: ~18-20% at restaurants; $1-2 per drink at bars and ~15% for taxi rides.

landmarks: Graceland
Elvis Presley's colonnaded mansion-turned-shrine draws pilgrims worldwide to tour its Jungle Room, trophy hall, and the quiet Meditation Garden where the King rests.
Beale Street
Neon-lit blues clubs, barbecue joints, and live music spill onto this legendary downtown strip, the beating heart of Memphis nightlife since the early 1900s.
National Civil Rights Museum (Lorraine Motel)
Built around the motel where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in 1968, this powerful museum traces the American civil rights struggle in unflinching detail.
Sun Studio
The tiny storefront studio where Elvis, Johnny Cash, and Jerry Lee Lewis first recorded, rightly billed as the birthplace of rock and roll.
Stax Museum of American Soul Music
On the site of the original Stax Records, this soulful museum celebrates Otis Redding, Isaac Hayes, and the gritty Memphis sound they created.
Memphis Pyramid
A gleaming 32-story stainless-steel pyramid on the Mississippi, now housing a colossal Bass Pro Shops with an observation deck offering sweeping river views.
The Peabody Hotel Duck March
Twice daily, five pampered ducks parade along a red carpet to the lobby fountain of this grand 1925 hotel, a beloved Memphis ritual since the 1930s.
Mud Island River Park
A Mississippi River peninsula featuring a walkable five-block scale model of the river itself, plus museum exhibits and skyline views from the monorail.
Big River Crossing
The longest public pedestrian bridge across the Mississippi lets you walk from Tennessee to Arkansas on a converted rail span with panoramic sunset views.
Shelby Farms Park
One of America's largest urban parks sprawls over 4,500 acres of lakes, trails, and meadows, complete with a resident herd of buffalo.

train.note: Amtrak's City of New Orleans is the only train, running once daily each way between Chicago and New Orleans via Carbondale, Memphis and Jackson. It calls at the handsomely restored Central Station on Main Street in the South Main Arts District, right in downtown Memphis and served by the MATA Main Street heritage streetcar, which was extended to the station in 2021. The timings are unhelpful - northbound in the late evening, southbound in the morning - and the run to New Orleans takes around eight hours. No international trains come anywhere near Tennessee.

bus.note: There are no international coach routes from Memphis; the nearest border is well over a thousand miles away. Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/), FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) and Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/) handle the long-distance runs, roughly three hours to Nashville, two and a half to Little Rock, five to St Louis and seven to eight to New Orleans. Buy online in advance - walk-up counter fares are markedly higher. Local MATA buses and the trolley connect the terminal area with downtown.

ferry.note: Memphis sits on the Mississippi but has no scheduled passenger ferry - the river here is crossed by bridge and used by barge traffic. The only boats carrying passengers are sightseeing paddlewheelers from Beale Street Landing and occasional overnight river cruise ships that call at the city as part of longer Mississippi itineraries.

half.name: Oxford
half.blurb: A Mississippi college town about an hour south, home to William Faulkner's Rowan Oak estate and the Ole Miss campus.

half.name: Tunica
half.blurb: A Mississippi Delta town about forty-five minutes south known for riverboat casinos along the Mississippi River.

full.name: Reelfoot Lake
full.blurb: Tennessee's only natural lake, formed by earthquakes in 1811 and 1812, with cypress swamps and wintering bald eagles.
